item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note: Moves the coil slowly along the bar. Too fast and impurities cannot keep up.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note1: A long threaded rod: turn it and things move in a straight line.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note3: The distance moved per turn is the lead (pitch). Speed = lead × revolutions. A 1 mm lead screw turned once a minute moves 6 cm an hour, turning a motor's spin into a slow, precise straight-line motion.
item.semiconductor-lab.lead_screw.note4: Around 1800 Henry Maudslay in England built an all-metal lathe whose tool carriage was driven by a lead screw, so accurate screws could be made identical again and again. The stages of today's chip lithography machines (ball screws) are its descendants.
block.semiconductor-lab.lathe.note1: A machine that spins material and cuts it with a tool to make round parts.
block.semiconductor-lab.lathe.note2: 750 W electric. Steel ingot -> rotary pump rotor (30 s). Recipe: 2 steel + lead screw + 2 iron + motor. The tool carriage is moved by the lead screw, far more precisely than by hand.
block.semiconductor-lab.lathe.note3: Around 1797-1800 Henry Maudslay in England built an all-metal lathe whose tool carriage was moved by a lead screw. The shaking of the hand was gone, and identical screws and parts could be made in any number. He is called the father of machine tools.
block.semiconductor-lab.lathe.note4: A lathe can remake its own lead screw more accurately (better screw -> better parts -> better screw). This cycle of machines making more accurate machines runs from precision engineering all the way to the nanometre stages of lithography machines.
block.semiconductor-lab.lathe.placeholde: Approximation: Maudslay's lathe was driven by hand, water wheel or steam; here by an electric motor. For now it only turns rotary pump rotors.
item.semiconductor-lab.pump_rotor.note1: A turned steel cylinder that spins inside a rotary pump.
item.semiconductor-lab.pump_rotor.note2: Turned from a steel ingot on the lathe. A part of the rotary pump [5-04]. It spins off-centre (eccentric), so the gap chamber grows and shrinks and pushes gas out.
item.semiconductor-lab.pump_rotor.note3: In 1905 Gaede built a 'rotary mercury pump' that moved air with a rotating part, turning the vacuum pump from a hand tool into a machine.
item.semiconductor-lab.pump_rotor.note4: The gap between rotor and casing is a few tens of micrometres. A larger gap lets gas leak back and spoils the vacuum, so the lathe's accuracy sets the pump's performance.
